what.definition: System design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data for a system to satisfy specified requirements.
what.summary: Learn how to design scalable, reliable, and maintainable distributed systems.
bullets: Scalability through horizontal and vertical scaling

why.summary: Good system design ensures your applications can handle millions of users while remaining reliable and easy to maintain.
why.impact: Poor design leads to system failures, downtime, and expensive rewrites.

props.title: Core Principles of System Design
props.heading: Scalability, Reliability, and Maintainability
paragraphs: Scalability is the ability of a system to handle growing amounts of work by adding resources. There are two main types: vertical scaling (adding more power to existing machines) and horizontal scaling (adding more machines to the system). Horizontal scaling is generally preferred for modern distributed systems as it provides better fault tolerance and flexibility.

Reliability refers to a system's ability to continue operating despite failures. Key concepts include redundancy (having backup components ready to take over), failover (automatic switching to a backup system), and replication (keeping multiple copies of data across different locations).

Maintainability is about how easy it is to modify, fix, or improve a system over time. Good maintainability comes from modularity (breaking systems into independent, well-defined components), documentation (clear documentation of architecture and decisions), and testing (comprehensive test coverage for automated validation).

The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can only guarantee two of three properties: consistency (all nodes see the same data at the same time), availability (every request receives a response), and partition tolerance (the system continues to operate despite network partitions). Most modern systems choose AP or CP based on their requirements.

choices.text: A distributed system can guarantee all three: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
choices.explanation: CAP theorem states you can only guarantee two of three properties.

choices.text: A distributed system can only guarantee two of three: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
choices.explanation: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can only guarantee two of three properties.

choices.text: A distributed system must sacrifice partition tolerance
choices.explanation: Partition tolerance is typically non-negotiable in distributed systems.

choices.text: A distributed system prioritizes availability over all else
choices.explanation: Different systems prioritize different properties based on their requirements.

questions.question: Which scaling approach adds more machines to handle increased load?

choices.explanation: Vertical scaling adds more power to existing machines.
Horizontal scaling involves adding more machines/servers to distribute the load.
Functional scaling is not a standard term in system design.
Linear scaling refers to proportional growth, not the approach of adding machines.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of redundancy in system design?

choices.explanation: Redundancy typically increases costs due to additional hardware.
Redundancy provides backup components that can take over in case of failures.
Redundancy may actually add latency due to synchronization overhead.
Redundancy makes architecture more complex, not simpler.

questions.question: Which is NOT a characteristic of good maintainability?

choices.explanation: Modularity is a key characteristic of maintainable systems.
Good maintainability requires documentation, not lack of it.
Testing helps ensure changes don't break existing functionality.
Clear interfaces make it easier to understand and modify components.

questions.question: In a distributed database, which choice prioritizes data accuracy over response speed?

choices.explanation: AP systems prioritize availability over consistency.
CP systems prioritize consistency and partition tolerance, ensuring data accuracy.
AC is not a common choice as it sacrifices partition tolerance.
This would mean the system is often unavailable, which is rarely desirable.

steps.title: Choose Consistency Model

choices.label: Strong Consistency
choices.description: All nodes see the same data at the same time

pros.title: Data Accuracy
pros.description: Users always see the latest data

pros.title: Simplicity
pros.description: Easier to reason about system behavior

cons.title: Lower Availability
cons.description: System may be unavailable during failures

cons.title: Higher Latency
cons.description: Waiting for all replicas to confirm

choices.whyThisFits: Best for inventory and payment systems
choices.whenToUse: When data accuracy is more important than speed

choices.label: Eventual Consistency
choices.description: System is faster, but users might see stale data briefly
choices.whyThisFits: Best for product catalogs and reviews
choices.whenToUse: When availability and speed matter more than immediate accuracy
